title: The Second World War in Europe & North Africa
description: From appeasement and the outbreak of war in 1939 through Blitzkrieg, Barbarossa and the desert war to Stalingrad, D-Day and the defeat of Germany in 1945.

notes.heading: Appeasement and the Road to War
notes.body: Through the 1930s Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles step by step: he rebuilt the army, sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland (1936), united Germany with Austria (the Anschluss, 1938) and demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking part of Czechoslovakia. Britain and France followed a policy of appeasement — giving in to demands in the hope of avoiding war. At the Munich Conference in September 1938, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain agreed Hitler could take the Sudetenland and returned home promising 'peace for our time'. Appeasement had reasons: memories of the First World War's horrors, fear of bombing, an unprepared military, and a belief that communism was the greater threat. But in March 1939 Hitler broke his promises and seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, proving he could not be trusted. Britain and France finally guaranteed to defend Poland. In August 1939 Hitler stunned the world with the Nazi-Soviet Pact, a non-aggression deal with his sworn enemy Stalin. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland; Britain and France declared war two days later.

notes.heading: Blitzkrieg and the Fall of France
notes.body: Germany's early victories rested on Blitzkrieg — 'lightning war'. Fast-moving tanks punched through enemy lines, dive-bombers attacked ahead of them, and motorised infantry followed to surround and destroy the defenders, all coordinated by radio. Poland fell in weeks in September 1939. Then came the 'Phoney War', months of inaction in the west, before Germany struck in spring 1940: Denmark and Norway in April, then the Netherlands, Belgium and France in May. The German attack through the Ardennes forest — thought impossible for tanks — split the Allied armies. British and French troops were trapped on the coast but around 338,000 were rescued from the beaches of Dunkirk in May–June 1940 by a fleet that included hundreds of small civilian boats. France surrendered in June 1940, just six weeks after the attack began. Britain now stood alone, but its new Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, refused to make peace: 'We shall never surrender.'

notes.heading: The Battle of Britain and the Blitz
notes.body: To invade Britain, Hitler first needed control of the air. In the summer of 1940 the German Luftwaffe attacked British airfields, ports and radar stations, and the RAF fought back in what became the Battle of Britain. Britain's advantages were crucial: radar gave early warning of raids; the Spitfire and Hurricane were excellent fighters; pilots flew over home territory, so those who bailed out could fight again; and German bombers were at the limit of their range. In September 1940, frustrated, Hitler switched to bombing cities — the Blitz. For months, London and cities such as Coventry, Liverpool, Glasgow and Plymouth were bombed at night. Civilians sheltered in Underground stations and Anderson shelters in gardens, children had been evacuated to the countryside, and people coped with blackout, rationing and the constant wail of sirens. Around 43,000 civilians died, but morale held. Unable to defeat the RAF, Hitler postponed invasion — his first major defeat — and turned east instead.

notes.heading: Operation Barbarossa: The Invasion of the USSR
notes.body: In June 1941 Hitler broke the Nazi-Soviet Pact and invaded the Soviet Union — Operation Barbarossa, the largest invasion in history, with over three million German and allied troops. Hitler wanted Lebensraum (living space), the USSR's grain and oil, and the destruction of communism. At first Blitzkrieg seemed to work again: Soviet forces were caught unprepared, and millions of soldiers were captured as German armies drove deep towards Leningrad, Moscow and the Caucasus. But the invasion stalled. The USSR's sheer size swallowed the attackers; supply lines stretched thousands of kilometres; Stalin moved entire factories east beyond German reach; and then the Russian winter arrived — German troops, still in summer uniforms, froze outside Moscow in December 1941. The invasion was also a war of racial ideology and extraordinary brutality in the east, where mass murder accompanied the armies. Barbarossa was a turning point: Germany was now fighting a war on two fronts it could not afford, against an enemy with far greater manpower and resources.

notes.heading: The War in North Africa
notes.body: Fighting spread to North Africa in 1940 when Italy, Germany's ally, attacked British-held Egypt from its colony in Libya. The stakes were high: control of Egypt meant control of the Suez Canal, Britain's vital supply route to its empire, and access to Middle Eastern oil. The small British army first drove the Italians back, so Hitler sent the Afrika Korps under General Erwin Rommel, the 'Desert Fox', whose bold tank attacks pushed the British back towards Egypt in 1941–42. Desert warfare was a new kind of fight — vast distances, scorching heat, sandstorms, and constant shortages of fuel and water brought by sea under air attack. The decisive moment came at El Alamein in Egypt in October–November 1942, where General Montgomery's Eighth Army, with better supplies and more tanks, defeated Rommel and forced him into a long retreat westwards. Days later, American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria (Operation Torch), trapping the Axis armies between two forces. By May 1943 all Axis forces in North Africa — around 250,000 men — had surrendered.

notes.heading: Turning Points: Stalingrad and El Alamein
notes.body: Two battles in late 1942 are often seen as the turning points of the war in the West and East. At Stalingrad (August 1942 – February 1943) Hitler ordered his army to take the city on the Volga that bore Stalin's name. The fighting was savage — street by street, factory by factory, through the winter. The Soviet commander, General Zhukov, held on just long enough, then surrounded the German Sixth Army in a huge counter-attack. Hitler refused to let them retreat; in February 1943 the survivors — about 90,000 men from an army of 300,000 — surrendered. It was Germany's first great defeat, and from then on the Red Army advanced westwards almost without pause. El Alamein, though smaller, mattered enormously too: it ended the Axis threat to the Suez Canal and began the push that cleared North Africa. Churchill summed it up: 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.' Together, the two battles showed that the initiative had passed to the Allies.

notes.heading: D-Day and the Defeat of Germany
notes.body: After North Africa, the Allies invaded Italy in 1943, knocking it out of the war, while the Red Army ground westwards and Allied bombers pounded German industry by day and night. The decisive blow in the west was D-Day, 6 June 1944: Operation Overlord, the largest seaborne invasion in history. Around 156,000 Allied troops landed on five Normandy beaches, supported by a brilliant deception campaign that convinced Hitler the real attack would come at Calais. After hard fighting — British and Canadians at Caen, Americans at Cherbourg — the Allies broke out, liberated Paris in August 1944 and pushed towards Germany. Hitler's last gamble, the Ardennes counter-attack (the Battle of the Bulge, December 1944), failed. In 1945 the Allies crossed the Rhine from the west while the Red Army closed on Berlin from the east. As Soviet troops fought into his capital, Hitler took his own life in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 7–8 May 1945 — VE (Victory in Europe) Day. The war in Europe was over; the war against Japan continued in Asia.

flashcards.definition: The British and French policy of giving in to some of Hitler's demands in the 1930s in the hope of avoiding another war, most famously at Munich in 1938.
flashcards.example: Chamberlain allowed Hitler to take the Sudetenland and declared 'peace for our time'.

flashcards.definition: The non-aggression agreement between Hitler and Stalin in August 1939, which secretly divided Eastern Europe and freed Germany to invade Poland.
flashcards.example: Hitler broke the pact by invading the USSR in June 1941.

flashcards.definition: Meaning 'lightning war': the German tactic of rapid attack combining tanks, dive-bombers and motorised infantry to break through and surround the enemy.
flashcards.example: Poland fell in weeks in 1939 and France in just six weeks in 1940.

flashcards.definition: The evacuation of around 338,000 British and French troops from the beaches of northern France in May–June 1940, helped by hundreds of small civilian boats.
flashcards.example: Churchill called it a 'miracle of deliverance' but warned that wars are not won by evacuations.

flashcards.definition: The air battle of summer 1940 in which the RAF defeated the Luftwaffe's attempt to win control of the skies, forcing Hitler to abandon his planned invasion of Britain.
flashcards.example: Radar, the Spitfire and fighting over home territory were key British advantages.

flashcards.definition: The German bombing campaign against British cities from September 1940 to May 1941. Around 43,000 civilians were killed; London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights.
flashcards.example: Civilians sheltered in Underground stations and Anderson shelters during night raids.

flashcards.definition: The German invasion of the Soviet Union, launched in June 1941 with over three million troops. It stalled before Moscow in the winter and turned into a disaster for Germany.
flashcards.example: The Soviet winter, vast distances and huge Soviet reserves defeated the Blitzkrieg.

flashcards.definition: German general known as the 'Desert Fox', commander of the Afrika Korps in North Africa, admired even by his enemies for his bold tank tactics.
flashcards.example: Rommel was finally defeated by Montgomery at El Alamein in 1942.

flashcards.definition: The British victory over Rommel in Egypt, October–November 1942, led by General Montgomery. It ended the Axis threat to the Suez Canal and began the clearing of North Africa.
flashcards.example: Churchill: 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.'

flashcards.definition: The brutal battle for the Soviet city from August 1942 to February 1943. The German Sixth Army was surrounded and surrendered — the turning point on the Eastern Front.
flashcards.example: Of about 300,000 men in the Sixth Army, only around 90,000 survived to surrender.

flashcards.definition: The Allied landings on five Normandy beaches on 6 June 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history, which opened the way to the liberation of Western Europe.
flashcards.example: A deception plan convinced Hitler the real invasion would come at Calais, not Normandy.

flashcards.definition: Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945 — the day Germany's unconditional surrender took effect, ending the war in Europe after Hitler's death and the fall of Berlin.
flashcards.example: Huge crowds celebrated in London and other Allied capitals while the war in Asia continued.

questions.stem: Which event directly caused Britain and France to declare war on Germany in September 1939?
choices: The Anschluss with Austria
The invasion of Poland
The Munich Conference
The remilitarisation of the Rhineland
questions.explanation: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France had guaranteed Poland's borders and declared war two days later — appeasement was over.

questions.stem: What was the policy of appeasement?
choices: Forming a military alliance with Germany
Giving in to some of Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding war
Bombing German cities to force surrender
Paying reparations to Germany
questions.explanation: Appeasement meant making concessions to Hitler — such as accepting the takeover of the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938 — in the hope that he would be satisfied and war would be avoided.

questions.stem: Why did Britain and France follow a policy of appeasement in the 1930s?
choices: They wanted Germany to rule all of Europe
Memories of the First World War, fear of bombing, military unpreparedness and the belief that communism was the greater threat
The League of Nations ordered them to
They had signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact
questions.explanation: Appeasement seemed reasonable to many at the time: both nations dreaded a repeat of 1914–18, their air forces were weak, and some saw Hitler as a barrier against Stalin's USSR.

questions.stem: What were the key features of Blitzkrieg tactics?
choices: Slow sieges of enemy cities lasting many months
Fast tank attacks breaking through lines, supported by dive-bombers and motorised infantry, coordinated by radio
Trench warfare along a fixed front line
Naval blockades to starve the enemy
questions.explanation: Blitzkrieg ('lightning war') combined speed and surprise: tanks punched through, Stuka dive-bombers attacked ahead, and motorised infantry surrounded the defenders. It defeated Poland in weeks and France in six.

questions.stem: Why was Dunkirk important for Britain in 1940?
choices: It was Britain's first naval victory
Around 338,000 troops were rescued, saving most of the British army to fight another day
It forced Germany to surrender
It brought the USA into the war
questions.explanation: Though a defeat, the Dunkirk evacuation saved the core of the British and French armies. Without it, Britain might have had to make peace; Churchill warned, however, that 'wars are not won by evacuations'.

questions.stem: Which factor was most important in the RAF's victory in the Battle of Britain?
choices: Britain had far more aircraft than Germany
Radar gave early warning, and pilots fought over home ground so those who survived could return to battle
The German air force refused to fight
Bad weather kept the Luftwaffe on the ground
questions.explanation: Radar stations along the coast detected incoming raids, allowing fighters to intercept efficiently. British pilots who bailed out landed safely at home, while German crews were lost — attrition the Luftwaffe could not sustain.

choices: The German invasion of Poland
The Allied landings in Normandy
The German night-bombing campaign against British cities in 1940–41
The evacuation of children to the countryside
questions.explanation: The Blitz ran from September 1940 to May 1941. London and cities like Coventry, Liverpool and Glasgow suffered heavy night raids; about 43,000 civilians were killed but morale did not collapse.

questions.stem: Why did Operation Barbarossa ultimately fail?
choices: The Soviet Union surrendered immediately
The USA attacked Germany at the same time
The USSR's vast size stretched German supply lines, factories were moved east beyond reach, and the winter caught German troops unprepared before Moscow
German soldiers refused to invade
questions.explanation: Early victories were huge, but distances swallowed the attackers, Stalin moved industry east and found endless reserves of men, and in December 1941 the offensive froze outside Moscow. Germany was now trapped in a two-front war.

questions.stem: Why was control of North Africa strategically important to Britain?
choices: It contained most of Britain's population
Losing Egypt would mean losing the Suez Canal — the supply route to the empire — and access to Middle Eastern oil
It was the only route for invading France
The gold reserves of the empire were stored there
questions.explanation: Egypt guarded the Suez Canal, Britain's lifeline to India and the Far East, and the region held vital oil supplies. That is why Britain fought so hard to hold it against Rommel's Afrika Korps.

questions.stem: Who commanded British forces at the Battle of El Alamein?
choices: Bernard Montgomery
Erwin Rommel
Dwight Eisenhower
Georgy Zhukov
questions.explanation: General Montgomery led the Eighth Army to victory at El Alamein in October–November 1942. Rommel commanded the defeated Axis forces; Zhukov was a Soviet commander.

questions.stem: Why is Stalingrad considered the turning point of the war on the Eastern Front?
choices: It was the first battle fought in winter
The German Sixth Army was surrounded and forced to surrender, after which the Red Army advanced westwards almost continuously until Berlin
It brought the USA into the war against Germany
It forced the Soviet Union to make peace
questions.explanation: In February 1943 the encircled Sixth Army surrendered — about 90,000 survivors from 300,000 men. Germany never recovered the initiative in the east; from Stalingrad onwards it was the Red Army that advanced.

questions.stem: How did the Allies help ensure the success of the D-Day landings?
choices: They attacked exactly where Germany expected
A deception campaign convinced Hitler the invasion would land at Calais, so German reserves were held back from Normandy
They waited until Germany had surrendered
They landed in winter when no one was guarding the beaches
questions.explanation: Operation Fortitude fed the Germans false information — dummy armies, fake radio traffic, double agents — so Hitler kept powerful forces at Calais while the real invasion hit Normandy on 6 June 1944.

questions.stem: A historian wants to argue that 1942–43, not 1944–45, was when Germany truly lost the war. Which combination of evidence best supports this?
choices: The fall of France and the Dunkirk evacuation
Defeats at Stalingrad and El Alamein, after which Germany was forced onto the defensive on land, plus growing Allied bombing and the two-front war it could not sustain
D-Day and the crossing of the Rhine
The Munich Conference and the Nazi-Soviet Pact
questions.explanation: Stalingrad destroyed a whole German army in the east and El Alamein ended the Axis threat in Africa — both in late 1942. After that Germany was permanently on the defensive, out-produced and fighting on multiple fronts.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events is in the correct chronological order?
choices: D-Day → Battle of Britain → Stalingrad → fall of France
Fall of France → Battle of Britain → Stalingrad → D-Day
Battle of Britain → fall of France → D-Day → Stalingrad
Stalingrad → fall of France → D-Day → Battle of Britain
questions.explanation: France fell in June 1940; the Battle of Britain followed in summer 1940; Stalingrad ended in February 1943; D-Day came in June 1944.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why Germany was defeated by May 1945?
choices: Germany ran out of soldiers in 1940
Germany was fighting a war on multiple fronts against enemies — the USSR, USA and Britain — with far greater combined manpower and industrial resources
The German people overthrew Hitler in 1943
Italy switched sides and invaded Germany alone
questions.explanation: Once Germany faced the USSR, the USA and Britain together, the balance of resources was hopeless: Allied factories out-produced Germany, bombing wrecked its industry, and armies closed in from east and west until Berlin fell.
